newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkish army warns of "life or death" Islamist row.
newsitem.headline: Turkish army warns of "life or death" Islamist row.

text.p: Turkey's powerful army lashed out at the ruling Islamists on Tuesday, but Prime Minister Necmettin Erbakan appeared unruffled at the latest military assault on his precarious rule and said he was ready for elections at any time.
A top general warned the military's struggle against an upsurge in Islamist activism was vital to the survival of the 73-year-old secular republic.
"Destroying fundamentalism is of life or death importance," General Kenan Deniz, a senior army commander, told a briefing for journalists designed to raise the military's political profile.

The generals, who in February demanded Erbakan's coalition clamp down on Islamists, have become increasingly suspicious the prime minister is stalling. Two conservative ministers resigned at the weekend in sympathy with the army.
But Erbakan, modern Turkey's first Islamist leader, shrugged off the latest army pressure.
"The army is completely loyal to democracy," Erbakan told MPs from his Islam-based Welfare Party. "Let no one make use of the army for their own purposes."
He challenged secularist political opponents, many of whom back the military, to early polls. "Today at any moment, whoever wants it, we are ready for elections," Erbakan said.

But he added that there was no alternative to his 10-month-old coalition with Deputy Prime Minister Tansu Ciller's conservatives. "The current government is the only solution and the only chance for Turkey. There are no alternatives," he said.
The generals, who have staged three coups since 1960, have led a chorus of secularist uproar against attempts by Erbakan to relax strict restriction on the role of Islam in public life.
They fear Welfare is planning to turn NATO member Turkey into an Islamic state like neighbouring Iran.

General Deniz blasted Tehran, with whom Erbakan has made a special effort to patch up strained ties, accusing it of seeking to undermine Turkey by sponsoring separatist Kurdistan Workers Party (PKK) guerrillas active in southeast Turkey.

"Iran...is continuing with its efforts to destroy the regime in the Turkish republic," said Deniz, a leader in the security forces' fight with the PKK. "It is known to have directed terrorist actions in Turkey."
Erbakan, known for his colourful rhetoric, was set to meet armed forces chief Ismail Hakki Karadayi in the afternoon, aides said.
"He is coming to see me and I will hug him," he told his MPs "The press will go crazy. I am saying this in advance so they don't have a heart attack."
Istanbul shares were little changed in late afternoon trade. The main index dropped 1.11 percent on Monday and 4.3 percent last week amid rising political instability and fear of snap elections.
The crisis has sent some political leaders scrambling to find a new government formula excluding Erbakan.
Leftist leader Bulent Ecevit was meeting other opposition leaders later on Tuesday for talks on forming an alternative, "Islamist-free" government.
Ecevit opened talks with Mesut Yilmaz, leader of the main opposition Motherland Party. Both are former prime ministers.

Initial secularist moves against Islamist activism were evident on Monday when police said they had closed down more than 20 buildings in two western districts where Islamists were holding illegal Koranic lessons.
Separately, a quasi-military court began hearing a case against the preacher at a mosque in the courtyard of Welfare headquarters where Erbakan and the party leadership often worship.
